name: Temazepam

lead: Temazepam is a short-to-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine prescribed for short-term insomnia. In recovery circles, longer sleep is tied to less puffiness, clearer skin and a fresher face.

It enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at GABA-A receptors, causing sedation. It was synthesised in the 1960s and marketed from the 1970s. It has been studied for sleep; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: It is used on prescription for short periods of insomnia, taken at bedtime. Users combine it with regular sleep habits, with any looks effect expected to follow from better nightly rest.

Reported risks include drowsiness, amnesia, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, and serious respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol. It is Schedule IV in the US and prescription-only.

angle.text: Temazepam is a prescription benzodiazepine for short-term insomnia. The chain is deeper, longer sleep, better overnight recovery, then clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It has been studied for sleep.

lead: Temazepam is a short-to-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic prescribed for short-term treatment of insomnia. It enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation, and is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[1][2]
Grokipedia reports it was synthesised in the 1960s and marketed internationally from the 1970s.[1] It has no appearance indication and no studies of appearance outcomes.

paras: The label indicates temazepam for short-term insomnia, and guidance typically limits use to roughly seven to ten days.[1][2] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline reviewed it among drugs for chronic insomnia.[3]

Reported effects include drowsiness, dizziness, anterograde amnesia and next-day hangover effects; combination with opioids, alcohol or other CNS depressants raises the risk of respiratory depression, coma or death.[1][2] A case-cohort study of US veterans on opioid analgesics examined benzodiazepine prescribing and overdose deaths.[4] Tolerance, dependence and withdrawal can follow prolonged use, and older adults show increased sensitivity.[1][5] It is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

A randomised trial compared behavioural and pharmacological therapy, including temazepam, for late-life insomnia.[6] Registered trials have examined temazepam at high altitude and in insomnia among people with HIV.[7][8] A matched cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality; observational designs cannot show causation.[9] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
